about: Tip and discussion posts for @gcanth, posted in this order on tip days. Edit any text here. Every post is numbered in the series named in 'series'. Each post: photo (an id from photos.json) for the first slide, kicker (small label), title, slides (each with h, and t or points), question (the last slide and the end of the caption), lesson (optional lesson id, adds a link line), tags. Type 'settings' adds a slide with the photograph's camera settings from photos.json. Nothing posts until its "approved" is true: change false to true once you have checked it. Posted ones are recorded in instagram-log.json as tip:<id>; to post one again, give it a new id.

posts.title: Golden hour is rarely an hour

slides.t: Near the equator the sun climbs steeply, so the warm, low light can be over in 20 minutes or so. In Scotland in winter the sun stays low all day, and on summer evenings the glow can run on for hours.

points: Look up sunrise and sunset for the exact place, not your home town
Arrive 45 minutes early and be set up before the light arrives
Stay 20 minutes after the sun goes for the afterglow and blue hour

posts.question: What is your favourite time of day to shoot, and why?

posts.title: The calm behind the camera

slides.t: I go out for the experience: being in the moment, in the flow, where time gets lost and the noise of everyday life is shut out. I speak from experience when I say it calms me.

points: Looking for a photograph keeps your attention on what is in front of you, not on what is in your head
Flow, being completely absorbed in what you are doing, tends to come when the challenge matches your skill
A large study in England linked at least two hours a week in nature with better health and wellbeing
Put your phone on silent and leave it in your pocket
Spend five minutes just looking before you take a photograph
Notice the sounds, the air and how the light moves
Go slowly: one place, one hour, a handful of frames

posts.question: Does photography calm you too? What does being out with a camera do for you?

posts.title: Thirteen seconds in Hamburg

slides.h: What a long shutter does in a city
points: Moving lights turn into lines
People walking through often vanish or leave a soft trace
Buildings stay sharp because they do not move
A tripod, or a wall to rest the camera on
The lowest ISO for clean shadows
A two second self-timer or remote, so pressing the button does not shake the camera

posts.question: Have you tried long exposures at night? What surprised you?

posts.title: You need an expensive camera

slides.t: Light, timing and composition do most of the work. This photograph of Lindisfarne was taken on a Canon 600D, an entry-level camera from 2011.

points: Very low light, where bigger sensors stay cleaner
Fast action, where focus speed counts
Very large prints, where more pixels help

slides.t: Ask what your camera stops you doing. If the answer is nothing much, spend the money on getting to better light instead.

posts.question: What is the oldest camera you still use?

posts.title: One focal length for a week

points: Pick one focal length: 35 mm or 50 mm are good choices
If you use a zoom, leave it there all week
Zoom with your feet instead

slides.t: With one view of the world you stop reaching for the zoom ring and start looking. You move closer, step back and find angles you would have skipped.

posts.question: Which focal length are you choosing? Share your favourite and tag @gcanth.

posts.title: Straighten the sea

slides.t: A sloping sea looks like a mistake, because everyone knows water lies flat. Even one degree out is noticeable.

points: Turn on the electronic level in the viewfinder or screen
Turn on a grid and line the horizon up with it
On a tripod, level the head, not just the legs

slides.t: Use the straighten tool in your editor's crop. Draw along the horizon and it rotates for you. You lose a little from the edges, so leave some room when you shoot.

posts.question: Does a slightly wonky horizon bother you, or is it fine in the right photograph?

posts.title: RAW or JPEG?

points: Far more room to recover highlights and shadows
White balance can be changed freely later
Nothing is thrown away by the camera
Ready to share straight away
Much smaller files
The camera's colour and sharpening are often very good

slides.t: Most cameras can save both. Use the JPEG when it is right and the RAW when you need to fix something.

posts.question: Which do you shoot, and has the other one ever saved you?

posts.title: Let the lines do the walking

slides.t: Anything that carries the eye through the frame: a road, a wall, a railing, a shoreline, a row of lights.

points: Start the line near a corner or the bottom edge
Make sure it leads to something worth arriving at
Get low or wide to make the line stronger
Watch that it does not lead the eye straight out of the frame

posts.question: Roads, rivers or railings: what is your favourite leading line?

posts.title: Cold camera, warm room

slides.t: Bring a cold camera into a warm room and moisture condenses on the lens and inside the body, just like a cold glass in summer.

points: Before you go inside, seal the camera in a plastic bag or close it in your camera bag
Let it warm up slowly for an hour or two before opening
Take the card out first if you want to start editing

slides.t: Batteries lose charge quickly in the cold. Carry spares in an inside pocket, and swap them as the one in the camera fades.

posts.question: What is the coldest place you have taken a camera?

posts.title: 400 mm in the desert

slides.h: What a long lens does here
points: Picks one shape out of a huge scene
Squeezes distance, so layers stack up on each other
Leaves out everything that does not help

slides.t: At 400 mm, 1/80 s is far slower than the usual handheld guide of one over the focal length. It needs a tripod or very good stabilisation, and a careful press of the button.

posts.question: Do you take a long lens for landscapes, or stay wide?

posts.title: ND filters without the maths headache

points: 3 stops: 1/125 s becomes 1/15 s
6 stops: 1/125 s becomes 1/2 s
10 stops: 1/125 s becomes 8 s
Compose and focus without the filter
Switch to manual focus so it does not hunt
Note the shutter speed, fit the filter, and work out the new time
Cover the viewfinder on long exposures to stop light leaking in

posts.question: Which strength do you use most: 3, 6 or 10 stops?

posts.title: Always use the rule of thirds

slides.t: The rule of thirds is a good habit, not a law. It stops everything landing in the middle by default.

points: Symmetry and reflections, where the centre is the point
A small subject in a lot of space, pushed right to the edge
Patterns that fill the whole frame

slides.t: Put things where you mean them to be. If you can say why the subject sits there, it is probably right.

posts.question: Rule follower or rule breaker?

posts.title: Trust the histogram, not the screen

slides.t: Camera screens are bright, and look brighter still at dawn or at night. A photo that looks fine there can be far too dark at home.

points: Left side: shadows. Right side: highlights
A tall spike against the right edge means lost highlights
Turn on the highlight warning so clipped areas flash

slides.t: Expose as bright as you can without the important highlights flashing. Bright skies at sunrise are the usual problem.

posts.question: Do you check the histogram, or go by eye?

posts.title: How much do you edit?

slides.t: I keep my editing light. Editing is my wife's passion more than mine. Two photographers, two different approaches.

points: Light editing keeps you honest about what you saw
Heavier editing can bring out what you felt
What matters is that it is your choice, not a habit

posts.question: Light touch or full edit? And how long do you spend on one photograph?

posts.title: Blue hour on your doorstep

points: Go out just after sunset, somewhere near home
Find lit windows, street lights or a bridge
Shoot while the sky is still deep blue, not black
Tripod, lowest ISO, f/8
Shutter speeds of a few seconds
White balance on daylight, or adjust it later from RAW

slides.t: Blue hour starts soon after sunset and usually lasts 20 to 40 minutes, longer in Scotland in winter. The best moment is when the sky matches the brightness of the lights.

posts.question: Share your blue hour shot and tag @gcanth. Where did you go?

posts.title: Shooting straight into the sun

points: Use a small aperture, f/11 to f/16
Let the sun just peep past an edge: a tree, a hill, a building
Wide lenses usually give the cleanest stars
Clean the front of the lens first
Take off any filter you do not need
Shade the lens with your hand, just out of frame

slides.t: Never look at the sun through an optical viewfinder, and do not leave the camera pointing at it for long. Use the screen to compose.

posts.question: Sunstars: love them or overused?

posts.title: Three copies, three places

slides.t: Keep every photograph you care about in three copies, each on a different storage point. For example: the computer, an external drive, and one somewhere else entirely.

slides.h: Why one copy must be away from home
slides.t: Fire, flood and theft take everything in the house at once. A drive at a relative's house, or cloud storage, survives that.

points: A sync folder is not a backup: delete a file and it vanishes everywhere
A backup you have never restored from is a hope, not a backup

posts.question: Be honest: how many copies of your photographs do you have right now?

posts.title: Where to focus in a landscape

slides.t: Focus about a third of the way into the scene. It is a fair starting point at f/8 to f/11, but it does not always work with a close foreground.

points: Focus on the nearest thing that must be sharp, or just behind it
Take the shot, then zoom in on the screen
Check the foreground and the far hills
Not both sharp? Close down a stop, or take two frames and blend them

posts.question: Where do you usually focus for landscapes?

posts.title: High ISO ruins photographs

slides.t: This one was taken at ISO 3200. Modern sensors handle high ISO far better than older ones did, and today's noise reduction is very good.
A little grain is easy to forgive. A blurred photograph cannot be fixed. If the shutter speed is too slow to hold, raise the ISO.

points: Expose well: lifting dark shadows later shows the most noise
Use the lowest ISO the light allows
Reduce noise first, then judge the sharpening

posts.question: What is the highest ISO you are happy to use?

posts.title: Tripod: always, sometimes or never?

points: Long exposures and low light
Slows you down, so you compose more carefully
Lets you blend frames that line up exactly
Weight on a long walk
Not allowed in many buildings
Image stabilisation now covers much of what it used to

posts.question: Which camp are you in? And what would make you leave it at home?

posts.title: Ten frames, one subject

points: Pick one ordinary subject: a door, a bench, a tree
Take ten genuinely different photographs of it
Change the height, the distance, the lens, the light

slides.t: The first two frames are the obvious ones. The interesting ones usually come after you think you have run out of ideas.

posts.question: Post your favourite of the ten and tag @gcanth. Was it the first or the last?

posts.title: Better reflections

points: Still water is calmest early in the morning
Puddles work after rain: get the lens close to the surface
Glass and shiny buildings in cities
A polariser can remove a reflection, so turn it until the reflection is strongest, or take it off
A centred horizon suits a mirror image
The reflection is often a stop or so darker than the subject, so watch the highlights

posts.question: Where is the best reflection you have found?

posts.title: Moving the camera on purpose

slides.t: Intentional camera movement: you move the camera while the shutter is open, turning a scene into lines and colour.

points: A slow shutter, around 1/4 s, gives time for the movement
A small aperture and low ISO keep the shutter slow in daylight
Strong, simple bands of colour, like sand, sea and sky, work best

slides.t: Pan smoothly along the horizon as you press the button. Expect most frames to fail. That is normal.

posts.question: Have you tried ICM? Art or just blur?

posts.title: Three habits for street photography

slides.t: With a 28 to 35 mm lens at f/8, focus manually at about three metres. Everything from about two metres to well past five will be sharp enough, with no waiting for autofocus.
Look for good light or an interesting background, then wait for someone to walk into it.

points: Smile if someone notices you
Delete a photograph if asked
Think hard before photographing people at their worst

posts.question: What is the hardest thing about street photography for you?

posts.title: Cleaning a lens properly

points: Blower first, to lift grit without scratching
Soft brush for anything left
Microfibre cloth last, with lens fluid for marks
Work from the centre outwards

slides.t: A breath and a shirt sleeve. Sand and salt trapped in fabric can scratch the coating.
Photograph a plain sky at f/16. Dark soft spots that sit in the same place on every frame are sensor dust, not the lens.

posts.question: Lens cloth in the pocket, or something else that gets you through?

posts.title: Woodland is easier on a dull day

slides.t: Bright sun through trees makes harsh patches of white and black. Cloud evens it out and colours stay rich.

points: Keep bright sky out of the frame
Use a longer lens to pick out one tree or a group
A polariser cuts glare on wet leaves and deepens greens
Mist is a gift: it separates trees into layers

posts.question: Woodland or wide open landscapes: which do you find harder?

posts.title: Phone or camera?

points: Always with you
Superb in good light
Clever processing does a lot for you
Better in low light and at long focal lengths
Real control over depth of field
Bigger files for printing

slides.t: A small compact sits in the middle. This one was taken on a Leica D-Lux 8, small enough for a pocket.

posts.question: What took your last favourite photograph?

posts.title: Real photographers don't edit

slides.t: Every digital photograph is processed. A JPEG has been edited by the camera: contrast, colour, sharpening, noise reduction. A RAW file has had none of that yet.
Not whether to edit, but who does it: the camera's settings or you. Film photographers made the same choices in the darkroom.
Adjusting light and colour is editing. Adding things that were not there is something else, and it is worth being open about.

posts.question: Where do you draw the line?

posts.title: Seeing in black and white

points: Strong contrast between light and dark
Shape and silhouette
Texture: bark, stone, sand, skin
Scenes where the colour is distracting rather than helping

slides.t: Shoot RAW and set the picture style to monochrome. You see black and white on the screen while you shoot, but the file keeps all the colour in case you change your mind.

posts.question: Do you decide on black and white when you shoot, or later?

posts.title: After the rain

points: Next time it rains, go out as it stops
Find a puddle with something interesting above it
Get the camera down, an inch or two above the water
Flip the result upside down if it looks better
Wait for ripples to settle
Street lights and signs make it glow after dark

posts.question: Wet weather photographs: share yours and tag @gcanth.

posts.title: Handheld in the city

points: 1/160 s is comfortably quick for a mid-range lens held by hand
f/5.6 keeps a good depth sharp without needing a tripod
ISO 640 is a small price for a sharp handheld frame

slides.t: Aperture priority at f/5.6 to f/8, auto ISO with a minimum shutter speed of about 1/125 s. The camera looks after the rest while you look at the scene.

posts.question: Auto ISO: do you trust it?

posts.title: Check three things before you go

slides.t: Where it rises and sets, and when. Light from the side shows texture; behind you it flattens.
It changes the whole coast. Holy Island at Lindisfarne is cut off twice a day, so the crossing times decide when you can go.
Some cloud catches colour at sunset. A solid blanket, or a clear sky, often gives less.

posts.question: What do you check before a shoot? Any apps you swear by?

posts.title: Say more with less

slides.t: One subject and a lot of empty space. The space is not wasted: it is what makes the subject stand out.

points: Use a long lens to cut the scene down
Look for plain backgrounds: sky, sand, snow, still water, a wall
Place the subject off centre and give it room
Fog and haze do half the work for you

posts.question: What is the emptiest photograph you have taken that still works?

posts.title: What got you started?

slides.t: My father-in-law. His influence got me going, close to thirty years ago, and I have been taking photographs on and off ever since.
The experience. Being in the moment, in the flow, where time gets lost and the noise of everyday life is shut out.

posts.question: Who or what got you into photography?

posts.title: Cropping for the feed

points: 4:5 portrait fills far more of the screen than a landscape
Square is safe for the profile grid
Wide landscapes appear small on a phone

slides.t: If you know a photograph is heading for Instagram, leave space top and bottom for a 4:5 crop, or turn the camera upright.
If cropping cuts something that matters, add a plain border instead. A whole photograph beats a damaged one.

posts.question: Do you crop for Instagram, or post the full frame?

posts.title: Sunny days are best

slides.t: Bright midday sun is often the hardest light to work with: deep shadows, bleached highlights, flat colour from above.

points: Woodland and waterfalls
Autumn colour, which glows under cloud
Portraits, with soft, even light
Detail and texture close up

slides.t: Go early or late, or look for shade, reflections and strong shadows that use the hard light.

posts.question: Best weather for photography? Wrong answers only, then real ones.

posts.title: A simple daylight recipe

points: f/11 keeps the scene sharp from front to back
1/250 s freezes the camera and any movement on the water
ISO 500 is the small price of having both

slides.t: Aperture priority, f/8 to f/11, and watch that the shutter stays at 1/125 s or faster by hand. It covers a lot of daylight landscapes.

posts.question: What is your go-to setting when you step out of the car?

posts.title: How slow for moving water?

points: 1/500 s: water frozen in drops
1/15 s to 1/2 s: soft, but still with texture
2 s and longer: smooth like silk
A tripod, and a two second timer
A polariser to cut glare on wet rocks
A cloth for spray, and check the lens between frames

posts.question: Silky or textured water: which do you prefer?

posts.title: A week in black and white

points: Set the camera or phone to show black and white
Keep it there for every photograph this week
Shoot RAW if you can, so the colour is still there later

slides.t: Without colour you start looking for light, shape and contrast. Many people find it changes how they see colour afterwards too.

posts.question: Share your best black and white of the week and tag @gcanth.

posts.title: Take the long lens for landscapes

points: Picks a small story out of a big scene
Stacks layers of hills and haze together
Makes distant things feel close and large
Use a tripod and turn stabilisation off if the camera advises it
Use a timer or remote
Heat haze softens distant detail: go early, when the air is cool

posts.question: What is the longest focal length you have used for a landscape?

posts.title: No photograph is worth it

points: Check the tide times and know your way off
Never turn your back on the sea
Wet, dark rock is usually slippery
Tell someone where you are going
Carry a torch for the walk back after sunset
Stay on paths: plants and nesting birds come first

posts.question: Any close calls you have learned from?

posts.title: Prime or zoom?

points: Smaller and lighter
Usually wider apertures for low light and soft backgrounds
Make you move your feet
One lens covers many situations
Fewer lens changes in dust and rain
Frame precisely without moving

posts.question: If you could keep one lens, which would it be?

posts.title: What a stop actually is

slides.t: A stop is a doubling or halving of light. Every exposure setting moves in stops.

points: Shutter: 1/250 to 1/125 s is one stop more light
ISO: 100 to 200 is one stop brighter
Aperture: f/8 to f/5.6 is one stop more light

slides.t: Change one setting by a stop, change another by a stop the other way, and the brightness stays the same. That is how you trade sharpness, blur and noise.

posts.question: What took you longest to understand when you started?

posts.title: Stop buildings falling over

slides.t: Tilt the camera up and the verticals lean inwards. The building looks as if it is falling backwards.

points: Keep the camera level and step back
Use a wider lens and crop away the extra ground
Correct it afterwards with your editor's perspective or Upright tools

slides.t: Point straight up and make the lines dramatic. A small lean looks like a mistake; a big one looks deliberate.

posts.question: Straight verticals or dramatic angles?

posts.title: Editing has replaced filters

slides.t: Graduated filters can often be replaced by taking two exposures and blending them, or by careful editing of a RAW file.

points: A polariser removes glare and reflections: no software can see what is under the surface
An ND filter gives a long exposure in daylight: editing cannot add real movement

posts.question: Which filter would you never leave behind?

posts.title: Find an abstract

points: Find a pattern, a curve or a repeat in a building near you
Fill the frame with it: no sky, no context
The viewer should wonder what it is
Stairwells from above or below
Car parks, balconies and windows
Shadows on walls at the end of the day

posts.question: Post it, tag @gcanth, and let people guess what it is.

posts.title: Timing the waves

points: 1/500 s or faster to freeze a breaking wave
1/4 s to 1 s for trails as water pulls back
Several seconds for a smooth, misty sea

slides.t: Watch a few waves first. Press as a wave starts to run back down the rocks or sand: that is when the best trails form.
Salt spray softens everything. Check and wipe the front of the lens often.

posts.question: Frozen waves or smooth sea?

posts.title: Exporting for Instagram

points: 1080 pixels wide is what Instagram shows
4:5 portrait: 1080 x 1350 pixels
Square: 1080 x 1080 pixels
Colour space: sRGB, or colours can look dull
JPEG, high quality
A little output sharpening for screen

posts.question: Does Instagram ever spoil your photographs? What helped?

posts.title: One tip you wish you'd known sooner

slides.t: Go back. The same place in different light, weather or season is a different photograph. Many of the best ones come on the second or third visit.
Beginners read these comments too. What would have saved you the most time, money or missed shots?

posts.question: What one tip would you give your younger self?
